title: Circuit Analysis
description: Kirchhoff's laws, dividers, nodal and mesh analysis, Thévenin/Norton, superposition, op-amps, C and L, first- and second-order transients, phasors and impedance, AC power, resonance, filters, transformers and three-phase power.

cards.title: A $10\,\Omega$ resistor carries $2\,\mathrm{A}$. How much power does it absorb, in watts?
cards.body:
$40\,\mathrm{W}$

By Ohm's law $V = IR = 20\,\mathrm{V}$, so $P = VI = 40\,\mathrm{W}$. The same result comes from $P = I^2R = 4 \cdot 10$ or $P = V^2/R = 400/10$.

Tip: pick the **power form** that uses the two quantities you already know.
Watch out: a resistor's $p = i^2R$ is never negative; it only absorbs power.
cards.searchQuery: resistor power I squared R watts

cards.title: Passive sign convention: current enters an element's $+$ terminal and $p = vi = -12\,\mathrm{W}$. Is the element absorbing or delivering power?
cards.body:
Delivering (supplying) $12\,\mathrm{W}$.

When current enters the $+$ terminal, $p = vi$ is the power **absorbed**. So $p > 0$ means absorbing and $p < 0$ means delivering. Absorbing $-12\,\mathrm{W}$ is the same as delivering $+12\,\mathrm{W}$.

Watch out: if current enters the $-$ terminal, use $p = -vi$ instead.
cards.searchQuery: passive sign convention power absorbed delivered

cards.title: $12\,\mathrm{V}$ is applied across $4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors in series. What is the voltage across the $2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor, in volts?
cards.body:
$4\,\mathrm{V}$

Voltage divider: $v_2 = V_s \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = 12 \cdot \dfrac{2}{6} = 4\,\mathrm{V}$. The $4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor takes the other $8\,\mathrm{V}$, since the larger resistor gets the larger share.

Watch out: the formula assumes nothing draws current from the midpoint. A load across $R_2$ must first be combined in parallel with $R_2$.
cards.searchQuery: voltage divider rule series resistors

cards.title: $9\,\mathrm{A}$ splits between $3\,\Omega$ and $6\,\Omega$ resistors in parallel. How much current, in amps, flows through the $3\,\Omega$ resistor?
cards.body:
$6\,\mathrm{A}$

Current divider: $i_1 = I \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = 9 \cdot \dfrac{6}{9} = 6\,\mathrm{A}$. The $6\,\Omega$ resistor carries the remaining $3\,\mathrm{A}$.

Watch out: in a **current divider** the *other* resistor appears in the numerator, so the smaller resistor gets the larger current.
Check: both branches see $18\,\mathrm{V}$, and $18/3 = 6$, $18/6 = 3$.
cards.searchQuery: current divider rule parallel resistors

cards.title: Node-voltage vs mesh-current analysis: which Kirchhoff law does each method apply, and what are the unknowns?
cards.body:
Node-voltage analysis applies **KCL**; mesh-current analysis applies **KVL**.

Node-voltage: KCL at each non-reference node, with the node voltages as unknowns ($N - 1$ of them for $N$ nodes). It works for any circuit.

Mesh-current: KVL around each mesh, with the mesh currents as unknowns ($B - N + 1$ of them for $B$ branches). It works for planar circuits only.

Tip: a voltage source between two non-reference nodes needs a supernode; a current source shared by two meshes needs a supermesh.
cards.searchQuery: nodal analysis versus mesh analysis KCL KVL

cards.title: Superposition lets you add the voltages and currents produced by each independent source acting alone. What can you NOT add this way?
cards.body:
Power.

Superposition works only for **linear** relationships such as $v$ and $i$. Power is quadratic ($p = i^2R$), so the power from two sources is not the sum of the powers from each source alone.

Example: two sources each give $i = 1\,\mathrm{A}$ through $1\,\Omega$. Together $i = 2\,\mathrm{A}$ and $p = 4\,\mathrm{W}$, not $1 + 1 = 2\,\mathrm{W}$.
Tip: add the currents or voltages first, then compute the power from the total.
cards.searchQuery: superposition theorem cannot add power

cards.title: Finding $R_{Th}$ by turning sources off: what replaces an independent voltage source, an independent current source, and a dependent source?
cards.body:
Voltage source $\to$ short circuit ($v = 0$). Current source $\to$ open circuit ($i = 0$). Dependent sources are never turned off.

With dependent sources present, either use $R_{Th} = v_{oc}/i_{sc}$, or turn off only the independent sources, apply a test source and take $R_{Th} = v_{test}/i_{test}$.

Key idea: Norton uses the same resistance, $R_N = R_{Th}$, with $I_N = i_{sc} = V_{Th}/R_{Th}$.
cards.searchQuery: Thevenin resistance turn off independent sources

cards.title: A source has $V_{Th} = 20\,\mathrm{V}$ and $R_{Th} = 5\,\Omega$. What is the maximum power, in watts, it can deliver to a load resistor?
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{W}$, when $R_L = R_{Th} = 5\,\Omega$.

At the match the load current is $I = 20/(5+5) = 2\,\mathrm{A}$, so $P_{max} = I^2R_L = \dfrac{V_{Th}^2}{4R_{Th}} = \dfrac{400}{20} = 20\,\mathrm{W}$.

Watch out: at maximum power transfer only **50% efficiency** is reached, because the source resistance burns as much as the load. Power systems avoid matching for that reason.
cards.searchQuery: maximum power transfer theorem load equals Thevenin

cards.title: What two rules let you analyze an ideal op-amp circuit that has negative feedback?
cards.body:
Two rules for an ideal op-amp with negative feedback:

1. No current enters either input: $i_+ = i_- = 0$ (infinite input resistance).
2. The inputs sit at the same voltage: $v_+ = v_-$ (the **virtual short**), a result of infinite open-loop gain plus negative feedback.

Tip: write KCL at the input nodes, never at the output node. The output current is an extra unknown that the op-amp supplies as needed.
Watch out: $v_o$ must stay within the supply rails.
cards.searchQuery: ideal op amp golden rules virtual short

cards.title: An inverting op-amp amplifier has $R_{in} = 2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $R_f = 10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$. What is its voltage gain $v_o/v_{in}$?
cards.body:
$-5$

The gain is $\dfrac{v_o}{v_{in}} = -\dfrac{R_f}{R_{in}} = -\dfrac{10}{2} = -5$. The $-$ input is a virtual ground, so the input current $v_{in}/R_{in}$ all flows through $R_f$.

Watch out: the input resistance of an inverting amplifier is just $R_{in}$, not infinite.
cards.searchQuery: inverting op amp gain Rf over Rin

cards.title: A non-inverting op-amp amplifier has $R_f = 4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ (output to $-$ input) and $R_1 = 1\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ ($-$ input to ground). What is its gain?
cards.body:
$5$

The gain is $\dfrac{v_o}{v_{in}} = 1 + \dfrac{R_f}{R_1} = 1 + \dfrac{4}{1} = 5$. The $R_f$/$R_1$ pair divides $v_o$ so that the $-$ input equals $v_{in}$.

Watch out: the gain is always at least $1$, and it is positive (no phase inversion).
cards.searchQuery: noninverting op amp gain 1 plus Rf over R1

cards.title: At DC steady state, an ideal capacitor behaves like what circuit element?
cards.body:
An open circuit.

At DC steady state $dv/dt = 0$, so $i = C\,dv/dt = 0$. No current flows, whatever the voltage across the capacitor.

Tip: for a DC steady-state problem, **replace every capacitor with an open circuit** and every inductor with a short circuit, then solve the resistive circuit.
cards.searchQuery: capacitor DC steady state open circuit

cards.title: At a switching instant, which cannot change instantaneously in an inductor: its voltage or its current?
cards.body:
Its current: $i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-)$.

An abrupt jump in $i_L$ would need an infinite voltage, since $v = L\,di/dt$. The voltage across an inductor can jump freely.

Key idea: the capacitor is the dual. Its **voltage** is continuous, while its current can jump.
cards.searchQuery: inductor current continuity switching

cards.title: In a first-order RC or RL circuit switched at $t = 0$, what is the general form of any response $x(t)$ for $t > 0$?
cards.body:
$$x(t) = x(\infty) + \left[x(0^+) - x(\infty)\right]e^{-t/\tau}$$

Here $\tau = R_{Th}C$ for RC or $\tau = L/R_{Th}$ for RL, where $R_{Th}$ is the Thévenin resistance seen by the C or L.

After $1\tau$ about $63.2\%$ of the change is done; after $5\tau$, more than $99\%$.
Tip: get $x(0^+)$ from the continuity of $v_C$ or $i_L$, and $x(\infty)$ from the DC steady-state circuit.
cards.searchQuery: first order circuit step response general formula time constant

cards.title: What is the impedance, in ohms, of a $1\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor at $\omega = 1000\,\mathrm{rad/s}$?
cards.body:
$-j1000\,\Omega$ (that is, $-j1\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$)

The impedance of a capacitor is $Z_C = \dfrac{1}{j\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{j \cdot 1000 \cdot 10^{-6}} = -j1000\,\Omega$.

Mnemonic: a capacitor's reactance is **negative**, $X_C = -1/(\omega C)$, and an inductor's is positive, $X_L = \omega L$.
Watch out: the capacitor's impedance falls as frequency rises.
cards.searchQuery: capacitor impedance 1 over j omega C

cards.title: What is the RMS value of $v(t) = 170\cos(377t)\,\mathrm{V}$, to the nearest volt?
cards.body:
$120\,\mathrm{V}$

For a sinusoid, $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt{2} = 170/1.414 \approx 120\,\mathrm{V}$. The angular frequency $377\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ is $60\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

Key idea: the RMS value is the DC voltage that delivers the **same average power** to a resistor.
cards.searchQuery: RMS value of sinusoid peak over root 2

cards.title: The charge entering an element is $q(t) = 5t^2\,\mathrm{mC}$ ($t$ in seconds). What is the current at $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, in mA?
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{mA}$

Current is the rate of change of charge: $i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = 10t\,\mathrm{mA}$. At $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, $i = 20\,\mathrm{mA}$.

Watch out: $q$ is in millicoulombs, so $i$ comes out in milliamps. Don't plug $t$ into $q$ itself.
cards.searchQuery: current is derivative of charge i dq dt

cards.title: Kirchhoff's current law (the currents entering a node sum to zero) follows from the conservation of what?
cards.body:
Charge.

KCL says no charge builds up at a node, so the current entering equals the current leaving: $\sum i = 0$. It is the circuit form of **conservation of charge**.

Key idea: KVL is the matching statement for energy.
cards.searchQuery: Kirchhoff current law conservation of charge

cards.title: Kirchhoff's voltage law (the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero) follows from the conservation of what?
cards.body:
Energy.

KVL states that $\sum v = 0$ around any closed loop. A charge that returns to its starting point has gained or lost no net energy, so this is **conservation of energy** (the electric field is conservative).

Watch out: KVL assumes no changing magnetic flux linking the loop.
cards.searchQuery: Kirchhoff voltage law conservation of energy

cards.title: Currents of $3\,\mathrm{A}$ and $5\,\mathrm{A}$ enter a node, and $2\,\mathrm{A}$ leaves through a third branch. What current, in amps, leaves through the fourth and last branch?
cards.body:
$6\,\mathrm{A}$

KCL at the node: current in $= 3 + 5 = 8\,\mathrm{A}$, current out $= 2 + I_4$. So $I_4 = 8 - 2 = 6\,\mathrm{A}$, leaving.

Tip: pick one convention (all entering is positive, say) before you write the equation.
cards.searchQuery: KCL node current sum example

cards.title: A $6\,\Omega$ resistor in parallel with a $3\,\Omega$ resistor, and that pair in series with $4\,\Omega$: what is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
cards.body:
$6\,\Omega$

Parallel first: $6 \parallel 3 = \dfrac{6 \cdot 3}{6 + 3} = 2\,\Omega$. Then in series with $4\,\Omega$: $2 + 4 = 6\,\Omega$.

Tip: for two resistors in parallel, **product over sum** is the quickest route.
cards.searchQuery: series parallel equivalent resistance

cards.title: What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms, of four $100\,\Omega$ resistors in parallel?
cards.body:
$25\,\Omega$

For $n$ equal resistors in parallel, $R_{eq} = R/n = 100/4 = 25\,\Omega$.

Watch out: parallel resistance is always smaller than the smallest branch.
cards.searchQuery: equal resistors in parallel equivalent resistance

cards.title: What internal resistance does an ideal voltmeter have, and what does an ideal ammeter have?
cards.body:
Voltmeter: infinite resistance (an open circuit), connected in **parallel** with the element. Ammeter: zero resistance (a short circuit), connected in **series**.

That way neither meter disturbs the circuit.

Watch out: a real voltmeter's finite resistance loads a high-resistance divider and makes it read low.
cards.searchQuery: ideal voltmeter ammeter internal resistance

cards.title: What determines the current through an ideal voltage source, and the voltage across an ideal current source?
cards.body:
The rest of the circuit connected to it.

An ideal voltage source fixes only its terminal voltage and supplies whatever current the circuit demands. An ideal current source fixes only its current and develops whatever voltage is needed.

Key idea: a source can **absorb** power (like a battery being charged) as well as deliver it, depending on the circuit.
cards.searchQuery: ideal voltage source current determined by circuit

cards.title: Name the four types of dependent (controlled) sources.
cards.body:
VCVS, CCVS, VCCS and CCCS.

- VCVS: voltage-controlled voltage source
- CCVS: current-controlled voltage source
- VCCS: voltage-controlled current source
- CCCS: current-controlled current source

They are drawn as diamonds. VCVS and CCCS gains are dimensionless, a CCVS gain is in ohms, and a VCCS gain is in siemens (like $g_m$ in a transistor model).
cards.searchQuery: four types of dependent controlled sources

cards.title: Using the passive sign convention, what is the sum of the powers absorbed by all the elements of a circuit?
cards.body:
Zero.

Energy is conserved, so the power absorbed by all elements sums to zero: $\sum p = 0$. Equivalently, the power delivered equals the power absorbed.

Tip: use this as a final **check** on a solved circuit; it catches sign errors in the sources.
cards.searchQuery: conservation of power sum of absorbed power zero

cards.title: A balanced delta (Δ) network has $30\,\Omega$ in each branch. What is each resistor of the equivalent wye (Y) network, in ohms?
cards.body:
$10\,\Omega$

For a balanced network, $R_Y = R_\Delta/3 = 30/3 = 10\,\Omega$. In the other direction, $R_\Delta = 3R_Y$.

Mnemonic: in the general case, each wye resistor is the **product of the two adjacent delta resistors over the sum** of all three.
cards.searchQuery: delta to wye transformation balanced

cards.title: A bridge has two dividers across one source: $R_1$ above $R_2$, and $R_3$ above $R_x$. It balances with $R_1 = 100\,\Omega$, $R_2 = 200\,\Omega$, $R_3 = 150\,\Omega$. What is $R_x$, in ohms?
cards.body:
$300\,\Omega$

At balance the midpoints are at the same voltage, so $\dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = \dfrac{R_x}{R_3}$. Then $R_x = R_3 \dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = 150 \cdot 2 = 300\,\Omega$.

Why: with no voltage across the detector, no current flows in it, so each side is just a voltage divider with the same ratio.
cards.searchQuery: Wheatstone bridge balance condition

cards.title: A $12\,\mathrm{V}$ source in series with $4\,\Omega$ is replaced by an equivalent current source in parallel with $4\,\Omega$. What is the current source's value, in amps?
cards.body:
$3\,\mathrm{A}$

The Norton current is $I = V/R = 12/4 = 3\,\mathrm{A}$, in parallel with the same $4\,\Omega$. The arrow points toward the $+$ end of the original voltage source.

Watch out: the two forms match **at their terminals only**. The internal power dissipation differs.
cards.searchQuery: source transformation voltage source to current source

cards.title: Node $a$ connects to ground through $4\,\Omega$, to a node held at $12\,\mathrm{V}$ through $2\,\Omega$, and to a node held at $6\,\mathrm{V}$ through $4\,\Omega$. What is $v_a$, in volts?
cards.body:
$7.5\,\mathrm{V}$

KCL at node $a$ (currents leaving): $\dfrac{v_a}{4} + \dfrac{v_a - 12}{2} + \dfrac{v_a - 6}{4} = 0$. Multiplying by 4 gives $v_a + 2v_a - 24 + v_a - 6 = 0$, so $4v_a = 30$ and $v_a = 7.5\,\mathrm{V}$.

Tip: write every branch current as (this node minus the neighbor) over $R$, and all terms leave the node.
cards.searchQuery: nodal analysis KCL node voltage example

cards.title: Nodal analysis: a voltage source connects two non-reference nodes. What two equations replace the KCL equations at those nodes?
cards.body:
The supernode KCL equation and the source's constraint equation.

1. KCL for the **supernode**, a closed surface enclosing both nodes and the source.
2. The source's constraint: $v_i - v_j = V_s$.

KCL at either node alone would need the source's current, which is unknown.
Tip: if the source connects a node to ground instead, that node's voltage is simply known.
cards.searchQuery: supernode nodal analysis voltage source between nodes

cards.title: Mesh analysis: a current source is shared by two meshes. What equations replace the KVL equations for those meshes?
cards.body:
The supermesh KVL equation and the source's constraint equation.

1. KVL around the **supermesh**, the larger loop formed by the two meshes that skips the current source's branch.
2. The source's constraint, e.g. $i_1 - i_2 = I_s$ (signs from the source's direction).

KVL can't pass through the current source because its voltage is unknown.
Tip: a current source in a branch belonging to only one mesh just fixes that mesh current.
cards.searchQuery: supermesh mesh analysis current source shared

cards.title: A planar circuit has 5 nodes and 8 branches. How many independent mesh (KVL) equations does mesh analysis need?
cards.body:
$4$

The number of independent loops is $B - N + 1 = 8 - 5 + 1 = 4$. In a planar circuit these are the meshes.

Tip: nodal analysis would need $N - 1 = 4$ equations here too, so pick whichever method has fewer unknowns or suits the sources.
cards.searchQuery: number of independent mesh equations B minus N plus 1

cards.title: A $24\,\mathrm{V}$ source in series with $6\,\Omega$ feeds a $3\,\Omega$ resistor, and the output terminals are across the $3\,\Omega$. What is $R_{Th}$ at those terminals, in ohms?
cards.body:
$2\,\Omega$

Turn off the $24\,\mathrm{V}$ source (short it). Looking into the terminals across the $3\,\Omega$, the $6\,\Omega$ and the $3\,\Omega$ are in parallel: $6 \parallel 3 = 2\,\Omega$.

Example: the Thévenin voltage is $V_{Th} = 24 \cdot \dfrac{3}{9} = 8\,\mathrm{V}$ in the same setup.
cards.searchQuery: Thevenin equivalent resistance example

cards.title: A network's terminals measure $12\,\mathrm{V}$ open-circuit and $3\,\mathrm{mA}$ short-circuit. What is its Thévenin resistance, in $\mathrm{k\Omega}$?
cards.body:
$4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$

$R_{Th} = \dfrac{v_{oc}}{i_{sc}} = \dfrac{12\,\mathrm{V}}{3\,\mathrm{mA}} = 4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$.

Key idea: the open-circuit voltage is $V_{Th}$ and the short-circuit current is $I_N$, so their ratio is the equivalent resistance. This works even with dependent sources.
cards.searchQuery: Thevenin resistance open circuit short circuit measurements

cards.title: A two-terminal network contains only resistors and dependent sources, with no independent sources. What is its Thévenin voltage?
cards.body:
Zero.

With no independent source there is nothing to drive the network, so its open-circuit voltage is $0$. It can be replaced by a single resistor $R_{Th}$, found with a test source: $R_{Th} = v_{test}/i_{test}$.

Watch out: the resistor can come out negative if the dependent sources are strong enough.
cards.searchQuery: Thevenin voltage network dependent sources only

cards.title: A $10\,\mathrm{V}$ source drives node $a$ through $2\,\Omega$; node $a$ has $3\,\Omega$ to ground and a $2\,\mathrm{A}$ source injecting current into it. Using superposition, what is $v_a$, in volts?
cards.body:
$8.4\,\mathrm{V}$

Voltage source alone (current source open): $v_a' = 10 \cdot \dfrac{3}{2+3} = 6\,\mathrm{V}$.

Current source alone (voltage source shorted): the $2\,\Omega$ and $3\,\Omega$ are in parallel, $1.2\,\Omega$, so $v_a'' = 2 \cdot 1.2 = 2.4\,\mathrm{V}$.

Total: $v_a = 6 + 2.4 = 8.4\,\mathrm{V}$.
cards.searchQuery: superposition theorem example node voltage

cards.title: Why insert a voltage follower (unity-gain buffer) between a signal source and a load?
cards.body:
To prevent loading.

A **voltage follower** copies the voltage ($v_o = v_{in}$) while drawing no current from the source. Its input resistance is ideally infinite and its output resistance zero.

Example: a high-resistance divider driving a low-resistance load would lose most of its voltage. With a buffer, the load current comes from the op-amp's supply instead.
cards.searchQuery: voltage follower buffer op amp unity gain loading

cards.title: An inverting summer has $R_f = 10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, with $v_1 = 1\,\mathrm{V}$ through $10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $v_2 = 0.5\,\mathrm{V}$ through $5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$. What is $v_o$, in volts?
cards.body:
$-2\,\mathrm{V}$

The output is $v_o = -R_f\left(\dfrac{v_1}{R_1} + \dfrac{v_2}{R_2}\right) = -10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\left(\dfrac{1}{10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}} + \dfrac{0.5}{5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}\right) = -(1 + 1) = -2\,\mathrm{V}$.

Why: each input current flows into the virtual ground and then through $R_f$, so the currents simply add.
cards.searchQuery: inverting summing amplifier output voltage

cards.title: Difference amp: $v_a$ drives the $-$ input through $R_1$, with $R_2$ from output to $-$; $v_b$ drives the $+$ input through $R_1$, with $R_2$ from $+$ to ground. What is $v_o$?
cards.body:
$v_o = \dfrac{R_2}{R_1}(v_b - v_a)$

By superposition, $v_a$ alone sees an inverting amplifier, $-\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}$. Alone, $v_b$ is divided by $\dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ and then amplified by $1 + \dfrac{R_2}{R_1}$, a net gain of $\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}$.

Watch out: it rejects the common-mode part of the inputs only if the two resistor ratios match exactly.
cards.searchQuery: difference amplifier op amp output formula

cards.title: An inverting amplifier with gain $-10$ runs on $\pm 12\,\mathrm{V}$ supplies. Ideally, what is its output, in volts, for a $+2\,\mathrm{V}$ DC input?
cards.body:
About $-12\,\mathrm{V}$: the output saturates.

Ideally the gain would give $-10 \cdot 2 = -20\,\mathrm{V}$, but the output can't go beyond the supply rails. It clips near $-12\,\mathrm{V}$ (a real op-amp stops a little short).

Watch out: the ideal-op-amp equations only hold while the output is **inside the rails**.
cards.searchQuery: op amp saturation supply rails output limit

cards.title: Which basic op-amp amplifier ideally presents infinite input resistance to its signal source: inverting or non-inverting?
cards.body:
Non-inverting.

The signal drives the $+$ input directly, which draws no current, so the source sees an ideally infinite input resistance. In the inverting amplifier the source sees $R_{in}$, because of the virtual ground.

Tip: that high input resistance is why the follower is a good buffer.
cards.searchQuery: noninverting amplifier infinite input resistance

cards.title: An inverting stage with gain $-5$ is followed by a non-inverting stage with gain $+3$, both built with ideal op-amps. What is the overall voltage gain?
cards.body:
$-15$

Ideal stages don't load each other (zero output resistance), so the gains simply multiply: $(-5)(+3) = -15$.

Watch out: with real op-amps, the bandwidth of the cascade shrinks and the stage outputs must stay inside the rails.
cards.searchQuery: cascaded op amp stages overall gain

cards.title: An op-amp integrator has input resistor $R$ and feedback capacitor $C$. What is $v_o(t)$ in terms of $v_{in}$?
cards.body:
$$v_o(t) = -\frac{1}{RC}\int_0^t v_{in}\,d\tau + v_o(0)$$

With a virtual ground at the $-$ input, the input current $v_{in}/R$ must all flow into the capacitor.

Tip: swap $R$ and $C$ for a differentiator, $v_o = -RC\,\dfrac{dv_{in}}{dt}$.
Watch out: practical integrators put a large resistor across $C$ so DC offsets don't drive them into saturation.
cards.searchQuery: op amp integrator output formula RC

cards.title: An ideal integrator has $R = 10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, $C = 1\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ and $v_o(0) = 0$. With a constant $1\,\mathrm{V}$ input, what is $v_o$ after $5\,\mathrm{ms}$, in volts?
cards.body:
$-0.5\,\mathrm{V}$

$RC = 10\,\mathrm{k\Omega} \cdot 1\,\mu\mathrm{F} = 10\,\mathrm{ms}$. For a constant input, $v_o = -\dfrac{v_{in}\,t}{RC} = -\dfrac{1 \cdot 5}{10} = -0.5\,\mathrm{V}$.

Key idea: a constant input to an integrator produces a **ramp** of slope $-v_{in}/RC$, here $-100\,\mathrm{V/s}$.
cards.searchQuery: op amp integrator constant input ramp output

cards.title: The voltage across a $2\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor rises at a constant $1000\,\mathrm{V/s}$. What current flows into it, in mA?
cards.body:
$2\,\mathrm{mA}$

$i = C\dfrac{dv}{dt} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \cdot 1000 = 2\,\mathrm{mA}$.

Key idea: a constant $dv/dt$ means a **constant current**. This is how a current source charges a capacitor linearly.
cards.searchQuery: capacitor current C dv dt ramp

cards.title: The current in a $5\,\mathrm{mH}$ inductor rises steadily from 0 to $2\,\mathrm{A}$ in $1\,\mathrm{ms}$. What voltage, in volts, appears across it during the rise?
cards.body:
$10\,\mathrm{V}$

$v = L\dfrac{di}{dt} = 5\,\mathrm{mH} \cdot \dfrac{2\,\mathrm{A}}{1\,\mathrm{ms}} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \cdot 2000 = 10\,\mathrm{V}$.

Watch out: use $\Delta i/\Delta t$ in amps per second; $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ is $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}$.
cards.searchQuery: inductor voltage L di dt ramp

cards.title: How much energy, in millijoules, is stored in a $100\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor charged to $10\,\mathrm{V}$?
cards.body:
$5\,\mathrm{mJ}$

$W = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(100 \times 10^{-6})(10^2) = 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J}$.

Watch out: the energy depends on the **square** of the voltage, so doubling $V$ quadruples the energy.
cards.searchQuery: energy stored in capacitor one half C V squared

cards.title: How much energy, in joules, is stored in a $2\,\mathrm{H}$ inductor carrying $3\,\mathrm{A}$?
cards.body:
$9\,\mathrm{J}$

$W = \tfrac{1}{2}Li^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(2)(3^2) = 9\,\mathrm{J}$.

Key idea: the energy is stored in the magnetic field and depends only on the present current.
cards.searchQuery: energy stored in inductor one half L i squared

cards.title: What is the equivalent capacitance, in $\mu\mathrm{F}$, of a $6\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ and a $3\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor in series?
cards.body:
$2\,\mu\mathrm{F}$

Capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel: $C_{eq} = \dfrac{6 \cdot 3}{6 + 3} = 2\,\mu\mathrm{F}$.

Watch out: capacitors in **parallel** add directly; series capacitors give a value smaller than the smallest one.
cards.searchQuery: capacitors in series equivalent capacitance

cards.title: A $12\,\mathrm{V}$ source drives $2\,\Omega$ in series with an inductor that has $4\,\Omega$ connected across it. At DC steady state, what is the inductor current, in amps?
cards.body:
$6\,\mathrm{A}$

At DC steady state the inductor is a short, so the $4\,\Omega$ resistor across it is bypassed. Then $i_L = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6\,\mathrm{A}$.

Tip: replace the inductor with a wire first, then see which elements are shorted out.
cards.searchQuery: inductor DC steady state short circuit current

cards.title: A $12\,\mathrm{V}$ source drives $2\,\Omega$ in series with a capacitor that has $4\,\Omega$ connected across it. At DC steady state, what is the capacitor voltage, in volts?
cards.body:
$8\,\mathrm{V}$

At DC steady state the capacitor is open, so the $2\,\Omega$ and $4\,\Omega$ form a divider: $v_C = 12 \cdot \dfrac{4}{6} = 8\,\mathrm{V}$.

Tip: the capacitor voltage equals the voltage across the resistor that is connected in parallel with it.
cards.searchQuery: capacitor DC steady state voltage divider

cards.title: At the instant a switch closes, how does an uncharged capacitor behave?
cards.body:
Like a short circuit.

A capacitor's voltage can't jump, so $v_C(0^+) = 0$. An element with $0\,\mathrm{V}$ across it and any current through it acts as a short.

Watch out: this is only for a capacitor with **zero initial charge**. A capacitor charged to $V_0$ acts like a $V_0$ source at $t = 0^+$.
cards.searchQuery: uncharged capacitor switching instant behaves like short

cards.title: What is the time constant, in seconds, of a series RC circuit with $R = 10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $C = 100\,\mu\mathrm{F}$?
cards.body:
$1\,\mathrm{s}$

$\tau = RC = 10 \times 10^3 \cdot 100 \times 10^{-6} = 1\,\mathrm{s}$.

After $\tau$ the capacitor has charged to about $63\%$ of its final value, and after $5\tau$ it is essentially full.
cards.searchQuery: RC time constant tau seconds

cards.title: What is the time constant, in ms, of a $50\,\mathrm{mH}$ inductor connected to a Thévenin resistance of $10\,\Omega$?
cards.body:
$5\,\mathrm{ms}$

$\tau = \dfrac{L}{R} = \dfrac{50 \times 10^{-3}}{10} = 5\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Watch out: for RL the resistance is in the **denominator**; for RC it multiplies. A larger $R$ makes an RL circuit faster.
cards.searchQuery: RL time constant L over R

cards.title: A $10\,\mathrm{V}$ source charges a $1\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor through $4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, with another $4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ directly across the capacitor. What is the time constant, in ms?
cards.body:
$2\,\mathrm{ms}$

With the source turned off (shorted), the capacitor sees the two $4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors in parallel: $R_{Th} = 2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$. Then $\tau = R_{Th}C = 2 \times 10^3 \cdot 10^{-6} = 2\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Tip: always find $\tau$ using the **Thévenin resistance** as seen from the capacitor or inductor terminals.
cards.searchQuery: time constant Thevenin resistance seen by capacitor

cards.title: A $24\,\mathrm{V}$ source is connected across an $8\,\Omega$ resistor. What current flows, in amps?
cards.body:
$3\,\mathrm{A}$

Ohm's law gives $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{24}{8} = 3\,\mathrm{A}$.

Tip: remember the three arrangements, $V = IR$, $I = V/R$ and $R = V/I$, and cover the unknown.
Watch out: Ohm's law is for the **resistor's own** voltage; in a series circuit that is not necessarily the source voltage.
cards.searchQuery: Ohm law current voltage resistance calculation

cards.title: What is the conductance, in siemens, of a $5\,\Omega$ resistor?
cards.body:
$0.2\,\mathrm{S}$

Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance: $G = \dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2\,\mathrm{S}$. Then $i = Gv$ and $p = Gv^2$.

Tip: conductances in **parallel add**, $G_{eq} = G_1 + G_2 + \cdots$, which is why nodal analysis is often written in siemens.
cards.searchQuery: conductance siemens reciprocal of resistance

cards.title: A $2\,\mathrm{kW}$ heater runs for $3\,\mathrm{h}$. How much energy does it use, in kilowatt-hours?
cards.body:
$6\,\mathrm{kWh}$

Energy is power times time: $W = Pt = 2\,\mathrm{kW} \cdot 3\,\mathrm{h} = 6\,\mathrm{kWh}$. In SI units that is $6 \times 3.6 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{J} = 21.6\,\mathrm{MJ}$.

Watch out: the **kilowatt-hour** is a unit of energy, not power.
cards.searchQuery: energy kilowatt hour power times time

cards.title: A Thévenin equivalent has $V_{Th} = 10\,\mathrm{V}$ and $R_{Th} = 5\,\Omega$. What is the Norton current, in amps?
cards.body:
$2\,\mathrm{A}$

The Norton current is the short-circuit current: $I_N = \dfrac{V_{Th}}{R_{Th}} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\,\mathrm{A}$, in parallel with $R_N = R_{Th} = 5\,\Omega$.

Key idea: this is a source transformation applied to the whole two-terminal network.
cards.searchQuery: Norton current from Thevenin equivalent

cards.title: Why can't you connect two ideal voltage sources of different values directly in parallel?
cards.body:
It violates KVL.

The loop through the two sources would need $V_1 - V_2 = 0$, which is impossible if $V_1 \neq V_2$. An ideal source has zero internal resistance, so the current would be infinite.

Example: a $12\,\mathrm{V}$ and a $10\,\mathrm{V}$ source in parallel leave $2\,\mathrm{V}$ across a zero-resistance loop.
Watch out: real batteries have internal resistance, which is what limits the circulating current.
cards.searchQuery: ideal voltage sources in parallel KVL violation

cards.title: What is the angular frequency $\omega$, in rad/s, of a $60\,\mathrm{Hz}$ sinusoid? Round to the nearest whole number.
cards.body:
$377\,\mathrm{rad/s}$

$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \cdot 60 \approx 377\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. The period is $T = 1/f \approx 16.7\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Watch out: $\omega$ is in radians per second and $f$ in hertz; don't mix them in $X_L = \omega L$.
cards.searchQuery: angular frequency omega 2 pi f 60 Hz

cards.title: What is the impedance of a $10\,\mathrm{mH}$ inductor at $\omega = 1000\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, in ohms?
cards.body:
$j10\,\Omega$

$Z_L = j\omega L = j \cdot 1000 \cdot 10 \times 10^{-3} = j10\,\Omega$. The reactance is $X_L = 10\,\Omega$.

Watch out: the reactance **grows** with frequency for an inductor, and it is a positive imaginary number.
cards.searchQuery: inductor impedance j omega L

cards.title: Write the phasor $10\angle 60^\circ$ in rectangular form $a + jb$ (two decimals).
cards.body:
$5 + j8.66$

$a = 10\cos 60^\circ = 5$ and $b = 10\sin 60^\circ = 8.66$. Back again: $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}(b/a)$.

Watch out: when converting back, check the quadrant; $\tan^{-1}$ alone can be $180^\circ$ off if $a < 0$.
cards.searchQuery: polar to rectangular phasor conversion

cards.title: A series RL circuit has $R = 3\,\Omega$ and $X_L = 4\,\Omega$. What is $|Z|$, in ohms?
cards.body:
$5\,\Omega$

$Z = R + jX_L = 3 + j4$, so $|Z| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\,\Omega$.

Watch out: resistance and reactance add as **vectors at right angles**, not arithmetically ($3 + 4 = 7$ is wrong).
cards.searchQuery: series RL impedance magnitude

cards.title: For $Z = 3 + j4\,\Omega$, what is the phase angle of the impedance, in degrees (one decimal)?
cards.body:
$53.1^\circ$

$\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{4}{3} \approx 53.13^\circ$. A positive angle means an **inductive** load: the current lags the voltage by $53.1^\circ$.

Tip: for a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle, remember $53.1^\circ$ and $36.9^\circ$.
cards.searchQuery: impedance phase angle arctan reactance resistance

cards.title: In an ideal inductor driven by a sinusoid, does the current lead or lag the voltage?
cards.body:
The current lags the voltage, by $90^\circ$.

Since $v = L\,di/dt$, the voltage is largest when the current is changing fastest, which is a quarter cycle before the current peaks.

Mnemonic: **ELI the ICE man**. In an inductor ($L$) the voltage ($E$) leads the current ($I$); in a capacitor ($C$) the current leads the voltage.
cards.searchQuery: inductor current lags voltage 90 degrees ELI the ICE man

cards.title: A series RLC circuit has $R = 10\,\Omega$, $X_L = 30\,\Omega$ and $X_C = 20\,\Omega$. What is $|Z|$, in ohms (two decimals)?
cards.body:
$14.14\,\Omega$

$Z = R + j(X_L - X_C) = 10 + j10$, so $|Z| = \sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} = 10\sqrt{2} \approx 14.14\,\Omega$.

Watch out: the capacitive reactance subtracts from the inductive one. The net reactance is $+10\,\Omega$, so the circuit is **inductive**.
cards.searchQuery: series RLC impedance magnitude net reactance

cards.title: A symmetric square wave swings between $+5\,\mathrm{V}$ and $-5\,\mathrm{V}$. What is its RMS value, in volts?
cards.body:
$5\,\mathrm{V}$

Squaring the wave gives a constant $25\,\mathrm{V^2}$, so $V_{rms} = \sqrt{25} = 5\,\mathrm{V}$. Its average value is $0$.

Watch out: the $1/\sqrt{2}$ factor applies **only to sinusoids**. A triangle wave has $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt{3}$.
cards.searchQuery: RMS value of square wave

cards.title: A sinusoidal voltage and current in a load have frequency $f$. By what factor is the frequency of the instantaneous power $p(t) = v(t)\,i(t)$ larger than $f$?
cards.body:
$2$

The product $\cos(\omega t)\cos(\omega t - \theta)$ contains $\tfrac{1}{2}[\cos\theta + \cos(2\omega t - \theta)]$, so the power oscillates at $2\omega$ about its average value.

Key idea: the constant term $\tfrac{1}{2}V_mI_m\cos\theta$ is the **average power** $P$.
cards.searchQuery: instantaneous power twice frequency sinusoidal

cards.title: A load draws $5\,\mathrm{A_{rms}}$ at $120\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$ and absorbs $480\,\mathrm{W}$. What is its power factor?
cards.body:
$0.8$

$\mathrm{pf} = \dfrac{P}{V_{rms}I_{rms}} = \dfrac{480}{120 \cdot 5} = 0.8$. The apparent power is $S = 600\,\mathrm{VA}$.

Why: $P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\theta$, so the power factor is $\cos\theta$, with $\theta = 36.9^\circ$ here.
cards.searchQuery: power factor real power apparent power

cards.title: A load has $P = 600\,\mathrm{W}$ and $Q = 800\,\mathrm{var}$. What is the apparent power $S$, in VA?
cards.body:
$1000\,\mathrm{VA}$

The power triangle gives $S = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2} = \sqrt{600^2 + 800^2} = 1000\,\mathrm{VA}$. The power factor is $P/S = 0.6$.

Watch out: apparent power is in **volt-amperes**, not watts, so equipment (transformers, cables) is rated in VA.
cards.searchQuery: apparent power power triangle P Q S

cards.title: What is the unit of reactive power $Q$? (It is not the watt.)
cards.body:
The var (volt-ampere reactive).

Reactive power $Q = V_{rms}I_{rms}\sin\theta$ measures energy exchanged back and forth with the inductors and capacitors, with zero average. It is positive for an inductive load and negative for a capacitive one.

Key idea: real power $P$ in watts, reactive power $Q$ in vars and apparent power $S$ in VA.
cards.searchQuery: reactive power unit var volt ampere reactive

cards.title: Is a typical induction motor load a leading or a lagging power-factor load?
cards.body:
Lagging.

An inductive load has its current lagging the voltage, which is called a **lagging** power factor (and $Q > 0$). A capacitive load has a leading power factor.

Tip: always state "lagging" or "leading" with the number, since $\cos\theta$ alone doesn't give the sign of $\theta$.
cards.searchQuery: inductive load lagging power factor induction motor

cards.title: What is the average power absorbed by an ideal inductor in sinusoidal steady state, in watts?
cards.body:
$0\,\mathrm{W}$

The voltage and current are $90^\circ$ apart, so $P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos 90^\circ = 0$. The inductor absorbs energy for a quarter cycle, then returns it.

Key idea: the same is true for an ideal capacitor. Only the resistive part of a load dissipates average power.
cards.searchQuery: ideal inductor average power zero

cards.title: How is a lagging power factor of an inductive load corrected, and what does the correction leave unchanged?
cards.body:
Connect a capacitor **in parallel** with the load. It supplies reactive power and leaves the real power $P$ unchanged.

The needed capacitor reactive power is $Q_C = P(\tan\theta_1 - \tan\theta_2)$, where $\theta_1$ is the old angle and $\theta_2$ the new one. The line current drops, which reduces losses in the supply wiring.

Watch out: the capacitor goes in **parallel** so the load voltage and the load's own operation don't change.
cards.searchQuery: power factor correction parallel capacitor

cards.title: How is the complex power $S$ computed from the phasor voltage $\mathbf{V}$ and current $\mathbf{I}$ (RMS values)?
cards.body:
$S = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}^*$

The asterisk is the complex **conjugate** of the current. Then $S = P + jQ$, so $P = \mathrm{Re}(S)$, $Q = \mathrm{Im}(S)$ and $|S|$ is the apparent power.

Watch out: forgetting the conjugate flips the sign of $Q$.
Check: for an inductive load with $\mathbf{I}$ lagging $\mathbf{V}$, the result has $Q > 0$.
cards.searchQuery: complex power S equals V I conjugate

cards.title: What is the SI unit of admittance $Y = 1/Z$?
cards.body:
The siemens ($\mathrm{S}$).

Admittance is $Y = G + jB$: conductance plus **susceptance**, both in siemens. A capacitor has $Y = j\omega C$ and an inductor has $Y = \dfrac{1}{j\omega L}$.

Tip: admittances of elements in parallel simply add, like conductances.
cards.searchQuery: admittance unit siemens Y equals 1 over Z

cards.title: A series RLC circuit has $L = 1\,\mathrm{mH}$ and $C = 10\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. What is its resonant angular frequency $\omega_0$, in rad/s?
cards.body:
$10^4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$

$\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10^{-3} \cdot 10^{-5}}} = \dfrac{1}{10^{-4}} = 10{,}000\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

Why: at resonance $X_L = X_C$, so $\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$.
Check: $X_L = 10^4 \cdot 10^{-3} = 10\,\Omega$ and $X_C = \dfrac{1}{10^4 \cdot 10^{-5}} = 10\,\Omega$.
cards.searchQuery: resonant frequency omega 0 1 over root LC

cards.title: An LC circuit has $L = 1\,\mathrm{mH}$ and $C = 1\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. What is the resonant frequency $f_0$, in hertz, to the nearest hertz?
cards.body:
$5033\,\mathrm{Hz}$

$f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{10^{-9}}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \cdot 3.162 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 5033\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

Watch out: this formula gives **hertz**; the one without $2\pi$ gives rad/s. Here $\omega_0 \approx 31{,}623\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
cards.searchQuery: LC resonant frequency hertz 1 over 2 pi root LC

cards.title: At resonance, a series RLC circuit's impedance equals what?
cards.body:
$R$, the resistance alone.

The reactances cancel ($X_L = X_C$), so $Z = R$: purely resistive and at its **minimum** magnitude. The current is maximum, $I = V/R$, and in phase with the source.

Watch out: a **parallel** RLC circuit is the opposite. At resonance its impedance is at its maximum.
cards.searchQuery: series RLC resonance impedance minimum equals R

cards.title: A series RLC circuit has $L = 1\,\mathrm{mH}$, $R = 5\,\Omega$ and $\omega_0 = 10^4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. What is its quality factor $Q$?
cards.body:
$2$

For a series circuit, $Q = \dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \dfrac{10^4 \cdot 10^{-3}}{5} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2$.

Key idea: $Q$ is the ratio of the reactance at resonance to the resistance. Voltage across $L$ or $C$ at resonance is $Q$ times the source voltage.
cards.searchQuery: series RLC quality factor Q omega L over R

cards.title: A resonant circuit has $f_0 = 10\,\mathrm{kHz}$ and $Q = 20$. What is its half-power bandwidth, in hertz?
cards.body:
$500\,\mathrm{Hz}$

$B = \dfrac{f_0}{Q} = \dfrac{10{,}000}{20} = 500\,\mathrm{Hz}$. A higher $Q$ means a narrower, sharper response.

Why: the half-power frequencies are the points where the current has fallen to $1/\sqrt{2}$ of its peak.
cards.searchQuery: resonance bandwidth f0 over Q half power

cards.title: An RC low-pass filter has $R = 1\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $C = 1\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. What is its cutoff (corner) angular frequency, in rad/s?
cards.body:
$1000\,\mathrm{rad/s}$

$\omega_c = \dfrac{1}{RC} = \dfrac{1}{10^3 \cdot 10^{-6}} = 1000\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, which is $f_c = \dfrac{1}{2\pi RC} \approx 159\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

Tip: the corner frequency is just $1/\tau$ of the same RC circuit.
cards.searchQuery: RC low pass filter cutoff frequency 1 over RC

cards.title: At the cutoff frequency of a first-order low-pass filter, the output amplitude is what fraction of the passband amplitude? Give a decimal to three places.
cards.body:
$0.707$, which is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

At $\omega = \omega_c$, $|H| = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 1}}$. That is a drop of $3\,\mathrm{dB}$, and half the power of the passband.

Key idea: the cutoff is also called the **half-power** or $-3\,\mathrm{dB}$ frequency.
cards.searchQuery: cutoff frequency gain 0.707 3 dB point

cards.title: A voltage gain of $10$ (as a ratio of amplitudes) is how many decibels?
cards.body:
$20\,\mathrm{dB}$

For voltage, $\text{gain}_{dB} = 20\log_{10}\left|\dfrac{v_o}{v_{in}}\right| = 20\log_{10}10 = 20\,\mathrm{dB}$.

Watch out: it is $20\log$ for voltage or current but $10\log$ for power. A gain of $\sqrt{2}$ is $+3\,\mathrm{dB}$ and $1/\sqrt{2}$ is $-3\,\mathrm{dB}$.
cards.searchQuery: voltage gain decibels 20 log10

cards.title: In a first-order RC high-pass filter, which component is in series with the input signal?
cards.body:
The capacitor.

At low frequencies the capacitor's impedance is huge, so the signal is blocked. At high frequencies it behaves like a short and passes the signal to the resistor, where the output is taken.

Tip: swap the two (the resistor in series, the output across the capacitor) and you get the **low-pass** filter.
cards.searchQuery: RC high pass filter capacitor in series

cards.title: A $10\,\mathrm{V}$ source charges an initially uncharged capacitor through a resistor, with $\tau = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$. What is $v_C$ at $t = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$, in volts (two decimals)?
cards.body:
$6.32\,\mathrm{V}$

$v_C(t) = V_s\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right) = 10\left(1 - e^{-1}\right) \approx 6.32\,\mathrm{V}$. This is the general step-response formula with $v_C(0^+) = 0$ and $v_C(\infty) = 10\,\mathrm{V}$.

Tip: at $\tau$ the capacitor has charged to $63.2\%$, at $2\tau$ to $86.5\%$ and at $3\tau$ to $95\%$.
cards.searchQuery: RC charging capacitor voltage after one time constant

cards.title: A $3\,\mathrm{mH}$ and a $6\,\mathrm{mH}$ inductor are connected in parallel with no mutual coupling. What is the equivalent inductance, in mH?
cards.body:
$2\,\mathrm{mH}$

Inductors combine like resistors: in parallel $L_{eq} = \dfrac{3 \cdot 6}{3 + 6} = 2\,\mathrm{mH}$. In series they simply add.

Watch out: this holds only when the inductors are **not magnetically coupled**.
cards.searchQuery: inductors in parallel equivalent inductance

cards.title: An ideal transformer has a turns ratio $N_1 : N_2 = 10 : 1$. If $120\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$ is applied to the primary, what is the secondary voltage, in volts?
cards.body:
$12\,\mathrm{V}$

$\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = \dfrac{N_2}{N_1}$, so $V_2 = 120 \cdot \dfrac{1}{10} = 12\,\mathrm{V}$. The voltage is stepped **down** because the secondary has fewer turns.

Key idea: voltage scales with turns; current scales **inversely**, so the power in equals the power out.
cards.searchQuery: ideal transformer turns ratio secondary voltage

cards.title: An ideal $10 : 1$ step-down transformer ($N_1 : N_2 = 10 : 1$) delivers $5\,\mathrm{A}$ to its load. What primary current flows, in amps?
cards.body:
$0.5\,\mathrm{A}$

$\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{N_2}{N_1}$, so $I_1 = 5 \cdot \dfrac{1}{10} = 0.5\,\mathrm{A}$. Power check: $V_1I_1 = V_2I_2$.

Watch out: the current ratio is the **inverse** of the voltage ratio. The side with more turns has higher voltage and lower current.
cards.searchQuery: ideal transformer current ratio primary current

cards.title: A $2\,\Omega$ load is connected to the secondary of an ideal $10 : 1$ step-down transformer ($N_1 : N_2 = 10 : 1$). What impedance does the primary source see, in ohms?
cards.body:
$200\,\Omega$

$Z_{in} = \left(\dfrac{N_1}{N_2}\right)^2 Z_L = 10^2 \cdot 2 = 200\,\Omega$. The impedance is scaled by the **square** of the turns ratio.

Why: $V_1 = 10V_2$ and $I_1 = I_2/10$, so $V_1/I_1 = 100\,V_2/I_2$.
Tip: this is how transformers are used for impedance matching.
cards.searchQuery: transformer reflected impedance turns ratio squared

cards.title: Why does an ideal transformer not work with a constant DC voltage on the primary?
cards.body:
A transformer needs a **changing** flux.

Induced voltage follows $v = N\,d\phi/dt$. With steady DC the flux is constant, so $d\phi/dt = 0$ and nothing is induced in the secondary.

Watch out: connecting a real transformer primary to DC is dangerous. Only the small winding resistance limits the current, and the winding can overheat.
cards.searchQuery: transformer does not work with DC changing flux

cards.title: In a balanced wye-connected three-phase source, each phase voltage is $120\,\mathrm{V_{rms}}$. What is the line-to-line voltage, in volts, to the nearest volt?
cards.body:
$208\,\mathrm{V}$

For a wye connection, $V_L = \sqrt{3}\,V_{ph} = 1.732 \cdot 120 \approx 208\,\mathrm{V}$. The line current equals the phase current.

Why: the line voltage is the difference of two phase phasors that are $120^\circ$ apart, which has magnitude $\sqrt{3}V_{ph}$.
cards.searchQuery: wye connection line voltage root 3 phase voltage

cards.title: In a balanced delta-connected load, each phase current is $10\,\mathrm{A_{rms}}$. What is the line current, in amps (two decimals)?
cards.body:
$17.32\,\mathrm{A}$

For a delta connection, $I_L = \sqrt{3}\,I_{ph} = 1.732 \cdot 10 \approx 17.32\,\mathrm{A}$. The line voltage equals the phase voltage.

Tip: wye has $V_L = \sqrt{3}V_{ph}$ and $I_L = I_{ph}$; delta swaps them.
cards.searchQuery: delta connection line current root 3 phase current

cards.title: A balanced three-phase load has line voltage $400\,\mathrm{V}$, line current $10\,\mathrm{A}$ and power factor $0.8$. What total real power does it absorb, in watts, to the nearest watt?
cards.body:
$5543\,\mathrm{W}$

$P = \sqrt{3}\,V_LI_L\cos\theta = 1.732 \cdot 400 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.8 \approx 5543\,\mathrm{W}$.

Watch out: here $\theta$ is the angle **between the phase voltage and the phase current**, not between line quantities, and $V_L$, $I_L$ are RMS line values.
cards.searchQuery: three phase power root 3 line voltage line current power factor

cards.title: What is the neutral current, in amps, in a balanced three-phase wye system?
cards.body:
$0\,\mathrm{A}$

The three line currents have equal magnitude and are spaced $120^\circ$ apart, so their phasor sum is zero: $I_a + I_b + I_c = 0$.

Key idea: for a balanced load the neutral wire carries no current, so it can be removed. An unbalanced load makes $I_n = I_a + I_b + I_c \neq 0$.
cards.searchQuery: balanced three phase neutral current zero

cards.title: A series RLC circuit has $R = 20\,\Omega$ and $L = 0.1\,\mathrm{H}$. What is the neper frequency (damping coefficient) $\alpha = R/2L$, in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$?
cards.body:
$100\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$

$\alpha = \dfrac{R}{2L} = \dfrac{20}{0.2} = 100\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

Key idea: compare $\alpha$ with $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$:
- $\alpha > \omega_0$: overdamped
- $\alpha = \omega_0$: critically damped
- $\alpha < \omega_0$: underdamped (rings)
cards.searchQuery: series RLC damping coefficient alpha R over 2L

cards.title: A series RLC circuit has $L = 1\,\mathrm{mH}$ and $C = 1\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. What value of $R$ gives critical damping, in ohms (one decimal)?
cards.body:
$63.2\,\Omega$

Critical damping needs $\alpha = \omega_0$: $\dfrac{R}{2L} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, so $R = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}} = 2\sqrt{1000} \approx 63.2\,\Omega$.

Watch out: a larger $R$ gives an overdamped (slow, no ringing) response, and a smaller $R$ rings.
cards.searchQuery: series RLC critical damping resistance 2 root L over C

cards.title: An underdamped RLC circuit has $\alpha = 300\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\omega_0 = 500\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. What is the damped natural frequency $\omega_d$, in rad/s?
cards.body:
$400\,\mathrm{rad/s}$

$\omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \alpha^2} = \sqrt{500^2 - 300^2} = \sqrt{160{,}000} = 400\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

Key idea: the response rings at $\omega_d$ inside an envelope that decays as $e^{-\alpha t}$. The ringing is slower than $\omega_0$.
cards.searchQuery: underdamped RLC damped natural frequency omega d
